title: A Uniform Power-of-Two Obstruction for Constructibility
description: Isolates the single arithmetic fact behind every classical compass-and-straightedge impossibility — that a number with an odd prime factor is not a power of two — and shows the same lemma governs both the Wantzel degree side and the Galois 2-group side of constructibility. Fully verified, 0 axioms / 0 sorries.

meta.author: Wantzel (1837); formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib

mathlibDependencies.description: For primes p, q: p ∣ q ↔ p = q — used to collapse 'q ∣ 2' to 'q = 2'
A prime dividing a power a^n divides the base a — reduces q ∣ 2^k to q ∣ 2
If every prime factor of n is p, then n = p^(length of prime-factor list) — the converse direction of the characterization
Every n ≠ 1 has a prime factor — extracts the odd prime witness for an odd d > 1
Cauchy's theorem: a prime dividing |G| yields an element of that order — concretely witnesses the group-order obstruction

prerequisites: Divisibility and prime factorization over ℕ
A prime dividing a^n divides a (Nat.Prime.dvd_of_dvd_pow)
Wantzel's degree criterion: a constructible number's minimal polynomial has degree a power of 2
Cauchy's theorem (existence of elements of prime order)

openQuestion: Is there a single, reusable arithmetic criterion that subsumes all of the classical degree obstructions at once, and that applies identically to the Wantzel degree side and the Galois group-order side of the constructibility characterization?

overview.historicalContext: Wantzel's 1837 criterion reduces the constructibility of an algebraic number to whether the degree $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]$ is a power of two. The three classical impossibilities — trisecting a general angle ($\cos 20°$), doubling the cube ($\sqrt[3]{2}$), and constructing a regular 7-gon ($\cos 2\pi/7$) — all follow because the relevant minimal polynomial has degree 3, and $3$ is not a power of two. The parent entry formalizes each of these three obstructions with its own ad-hoc proof that $3 \neq 2^k$. The full Wantzel–Galois characterization sharpens necessity to a biconditional: $\alpha$ is constructible iff the Galois group of its minimal polynomial is a 2-group, i.e. has order $2^k$. Both sides — degree and group order — are statements that a particular natural number is a power of two, so the obstruction to constructibility is, in both cases, the presence of an odd prime factor.
overview.problemStatement: Extract the common arithmetic core of the classical constructibility obstructions as a single Lean lemma, prove the full characterization of powers of two, and show the identical lemma drives both the degree predicate `DegreePowerOfTwo p` (Wantzel necessity) and the group-order predicate `IsTwoGroup G` (Galois sufficiency).
overview.proofStrategy: (1) Define `IsPowTwo d := ∃ k, d = 2^k`. (2) Prove the core obstruction `not_isPowTwo_of_odd_prime_dvd`: an odd prime dividing d forces d ≠ 2^k, since q ∣ 2^k ⟹ q ∣ 2 ⟹ q = 2. (3) Prove the full characterization `IsPowTwo d ↔ (every prime factor of d is 2)` via `Nat.eq_prime_pow_of_unique_prime_dvd`. (4) Specialize to polynomial degree: `DegreePowerOfTwo p` is `IsPowTwo p.natDegree`, giving a uniform `not_degreePowerOfTwo_of_natDegree_three` that covers all three classical degree-3 cases, plus a new degree-5 case (regular 11-gon). (5) Specialize to group order: `IsTwoGroup G` is `IsPowTwo (Fintype.card G)`, giving `not_isTwoGroup_of_odd_prime_dvd` from the same lemma, with Cauchy's theorem providing a concrete witnessing element.
keyInsights: The entire content of 'degree d is not a power of two' is the single fact 'd has an odd prime factor' — `q ∣ 2^k ⟹ q ∣ 2 ⟹ q = 2` is the whole proof, with no case analysis on k.

Both the Wantzel degree predicate and the Galois 2-group predicate are *definitionally* `IsPowTwo` applied to a natural number (`p.natDegree` resp. `Fintype.card G`), so one arithmetic lemma serves both sides of the constructibility characterization.

The parent's three separate `interval_cases k <;> simp_all` proofs become a single instance of `not_degreePowerOfTwo_of_natDegree_three`; the criterion extends for free to degree 5 (regular 11-gon) and any odd-prime degree.

On the group side, Cauchy's theorem (`exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card`) turns the abstract obstruction into a concrete witness: an element whose order is the offending odd prime cannot exist in a 2-group.

The obstruction is an odd prime *factor*, not an odd degree — so it also catches even composite degrees. `not_isPowTwo_six` uses 3 ∣ 6: a degree need not be odd to fail Wantzel, only to carry an odd prime factor. This is strictly stronger than both the parent's degree-3 arguments and the naive 'odd degree ⟹ non-constructible' heuristic — e.g. cos(2π/13) has an even degree-6 minimal polynomial (φ(13)/2 = 6 = 2·3) yet is non-constructible.

A prime dividing a^n divides a

sections.title: Header: a single arithmetic obstruction for both sides
sections.summary: Module docstring. States the parent's open question — the three classical impossibilities (angle trisection, cube doubling, regular 7-gon) are each dispatched by their own ad-hoc `interval_cases` argument; is there one reusable criterion covering both the degree side and the Galois-group-order side of the Wantzel–Galois iff? Answers: the whole content of 'not a power of two' is having an odd prime factor (not_isPowTwo_of_odd_prime_dvd), and since both DegreePowerOfTwo and IsTwoGroup are definitionally IsPowTwo applied to a natural number, this single lemma serves both the degree obstruction and the Galois-side mirror. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.
sections.mathContext: Both `DegreePowerOfTwo` (Wantzel, on `p.natDegree`) and `IsTwoGroup` (Galois, on `Fintype.card G`) unfold to the same predicate `IsPowTwo` on a natural number, so `not_isPowTwo_of_odd_prime_dvd` — a number with an odd prime factor is not a power of two — simultaneously obstructs both directions of the Wantzel–Galois characterization.

sections.title: Part 1: The power-of-two predicate and its core obstruction
sections.summary: Defines IsPowTwo and proves the core obstruction (odd prime factor ⟹ not a power of two), the full characterization (only prime factor is 2), the odd-greater-than-one corollary, and the concrete instances for 3, 5, 6.

sections.title: Part 2: Wantzel degree side
sections.summary: Specializes the obstruction to polynomial degree (DegreePowerOfTwo), giving a uniform criterion that recovers the three classical degree-3 impossibilities and a new degree-5 case.

sections.title: Part 3: Galois-group side (the sufficiency mirror)
sections.summary: Specializes the same obstruction to group order (IsTwoGroup), shows the two predicates share one arithmetic core, and gives a Cauchy-theorem witness for the obstruction.

sections.title: Part 4: Summary
sections.summary: Summary of the arithmetic core, the Wantzel degree side, and the Galois group side, with the unifying contribution.

conclusion.summary: Refactors the parent's three independent degree obstructions into instances of a single reusable lemma — that a number with an odd prime factor is not a power of two — proves the full characterization of powers of two, and exhibits the identical lemma governing the Galois-group-order side of the Wantzel–Galois criterion. The file is fully machine-checked: 0 axioms, 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: Clarifies why 'power of two' is the shared invariant on both sides of the constructibility characterization: the degree side and the Galois-group side are the same arithmetic statement about different natural numbers. The uniform criterion extends the parent's degree-3 cases (trisection, cube doubling, 7-gon) to degree 5 (regular 11-gon) and any odd-prime degree at no extra cost, and the group-side lemma is the obstruction the sufficiency half of `wantzel_galois_iff` rests on.
openQuestions: Can the degree-side and group-side obstructions be merged into the full `wantzel_galois_iff` biconditional by supplying the Galois correspondence linking `p.natDegree ∣ Fintype.card p.Gal` for separable irreducible p?
Can `not_degreePowerOfTwo_of_natDegree_five` be discharged against a concrete minimal polynomial of cos(2π/11) to formally close the regular 11-gon impossibility?

crossReferences.description: Parent: formalizes the Wantzel degree criterion with three separate degree-3 impossibility proofs and states the Galois characterization. This entry isolates their common arithmetic core into one reusable lemma serving both the degree and group-order sides.

Abel–Ruffini uses Galois-group structure (solvability) to prove insolvability of the quintic; here the Galois-group structure at issue is being a 2-group, obstructed by the same odd-prime-factor lemma.

The concrete group-side witness of this uniform obstruction: the Galois group of 8X³ − 6X − 1 (the minimal polynomial of cos 20°) over ℚ has order 3. Because 3 carries an odd prime factor it is not a power of two — exactly the arithmetic fact isolated here — so cos 20° is non-constructible and the 60° angle cannot be trisected. It instantiates the 'Galois 2-group side' with a specific polynomial.

The arithmetic Gauss–Wantzel criterion: a regular n-gon is constructible iff φ(n) is a power of two. This entry's power-of-two obstruction is the necessity engine — whenever φ(n) has an odd prime factor the n-gon is non-constructible. Feeding φ(11) = 10 (odd factor 5) into that criterion is precisely what would close this entry's second open question on the regular 11-gon.

A sibling under the same parent covering the opposite (sufficiency) direction: the 2-group backbone — every finite 2-group is nilpotent, hence solvable, with a normal subgroup of index 2. This entry supplies the necessity obstruction (an odd prime factor forces a non-power-of-two order, blocking constructibility); the sibling supplies the group-side backbone of the converse. Together they are the two halves this entry's first open question proposes to merge into wantzel_galois_iff.

mainTheorems.name: not_isPowTwo_of_odd_prime_dvd
mainTheorems.description: The single arithmetic obstruction: if an odd prime q divides d, then d is not a power of two. Proof: q ∣ 2^k forces q ∣ 2 (Nat.Prime.dvd_of_dvd_pow), hence q = 2 (Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq), contradicting q ≠ 2. This one fact underlies every classical compass-and-straightedge impossibility.
mainTheorems.leanType: {d q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (hdvd : q ∣ d) → ¬ IsPowTwo d

mainTheorems.name: isPowTwo_iff_unique_prime_two
mainTheorems.description: Full characterization: a positive natural number is a power of two iff its only prime factor is 2. Forward direction reuses the core obstruction; converse uses Nat.eq_prime_pow_of_unique_prime_dvd to reconstruct d = 2^(length of its prime-factor list).
mainTheorems.leanType: {d : ℕ} (hd : d ≠ 0) → (IsPowTwo d ↔ ∀ q, q.Prime → q ∣ d → q = 2)

mainTheorems.name: not_isPowTwo_of_odd_gt_one
mainTheorems.description: An odd number greater than one is never a power of two. Extracts a prime factor q (Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd), shows q ≠ 2 by parity (omega), then applies the core obstruction.
mainTheorems.leanType: {d : ℕ} (hodd : Odd d) (hgt : 1 < d) → ¬ IsPowTwo d

mainTheorems.name: not_degreePowerOfTwo_of_natDegree_three
mainTheorems.description: The uniform replacement for the parent's three separate proofs: any polynomial of degree 3 fails the Wantzel condition. Covers angle trisection (cos 20°), cube doubling (∛2), and the regular 7-gon (cos 2π/7) in one line via not_isPowTwo_three.

mainTheorems.name: not_degreePowerOfTwo_of_natDegree_five
mainTheorems.description: A new case the parent does not cover: any degree-5 polynomial fails the Wantzel condition — e.g. cos(2π/11), giving the non-constructibility of the regular 11-gon by the same mechanism.

mainTheorems.name: not_isTwoGroup_of_odd_prime_dvd
mainTheorems.description: The Galois-side mirror: a finite group whose order is divisible by an odd prime is not a 2-group. Literally the same lemma as not_isPowTwo_of_odd_prime_dvd applied to Fintype.card G — the obstruction the sufficiency half of the Wantzel–Galois criterion turns on.
mainTheorems.leanType: {G : Type*} [Group G] [Fintype G] {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (hdvd : q ∣ Fintype.card G) → ¬ IsTwoGroup G

mainTheorems.name: exists_orderOf_eq_of_prime_dvd_card
mainTheorems.description: Cauchy's theorem packaged for this setting: whenever a prime q divides |G|, the group contains an element of order q. Applied to an odd prime divisor, this concretely witnesses the failure of the 2-group property.
mainTheorems.leanType: {G : Type*} [Group G] [Fintype G] {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) (hdvd : q ∣ Fintype.card G) → ∃ g : G, orderOf g = q
